items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: If a stock falls 50% then rises 50%, you've LOST money
items.claim: Stock at 100. Falls 50%: now 50. Rises 50%: now 75. Two equal-percentage moves in opposite directions don't cancel.

options.text: Percentages are RATIOS, not amounts. The 50% drop reduces the base; the subsequent 50% rise is on a smaller base. To recover from a -50% loss you need a +100% gain

items.reveal:
To go from x to y, percentage change is (y - x) / x.

Loss of L percent: new value = old * (1 - L/100).
Gain of G percent: new value = old * (1 + G/100).

For symmetric percent moves NOT to cancel, multiply: (1 - 0.5)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Always less than 1 if the magnitude is the same.

Recovery table:
- Lose 10%: need 11.1% to recover.
- Lose 25%: need 33.3% to recover.
- Lose 50%: need 100% to recover.
- Lose 75%: need 300% to recover.
- Lose 90%: need 900% to recover.

Applications:
- Drawdowns in investing: deep losses require enormous gains to recover. A 50% bear market loss takes years of strong returns to break even.
- Discounted prices then surcharged: 50% off followed by 50% on actually leaves you at 75% of original price (consumer gets a deal).
- Inflation: 10% inflation for 7 years halves purchasing power, even though 70% < 100%.

Geometric vs arithmetic mean: a stock returning +50%, -50%, +50%, -50% has arithmetic mean return 0% but geometric (actual) mean of ((1.5 * 0.5 * 1.5 * 0.5)^0.25 - 1) = -13.4%/period.
items.why: Percentages feel symmetric. They're multiplicative ratios that don't cancel directly. Anyone interpreting investment returns, weight changes, price comparisons or compound growth without realising this misreads the data.

items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.
